Define a demographic process for FINN

Source: R/Processes_utils.R
createProcess.Rd

Configures one demographic process (growth, mortality, regeneration or competition) for use as mortality_process, growth_process, regeneration_process, or competition_process in finn(), either as a fully mechanistic process with an explicit, interpretable functional form, or – if hidden is supplied – as the first ("Level 1") level of hybridization described by Pichler & Käber (2026): only the process' environmental-response function is replaced by a small feed-forward neural network, while the rest of the process equation remains mechanistic. To replace the entire process equation with a neural network ("Level 2"), use createHybrid() instead.

Usage

createProcess(
  formula = NULL,
  func,
  initSpecies = NULL,
  initEnv = NULL,
  hidden = NULL,
  optimizeSpecies = FALSE,
  optimizeEnv = TRUE,
  inputNN = NULL,
  outputNN = NULL,
  dispersion_parameter = 1,
  NN = NULL,
  upper = NULL,
  lower = NULL,
  dropout = 0,
  sample_regeneration = TRUE,
  n_quantiles = 10L,
  continuous = FALSE,
  light_mask = TRUE,
  custom_parameters = NULL,
  mortality_draw = c("binomial", "bernoulli", "poisson", "gamma"),
  regeneration_sampler = c("refined", "gaussian"),
  growth_scale = NULL,
  cap = c("all", "species"),
  prior = "max_obs_recruits",
  prior_lambda = 0.1,
  theta_floor = 0.5,
  optimizeTheta = TRUE,
  mortality_floor = 0.001,
  mortality_ceiling = 0.999,
  reg_floor = 0.001
)

Arguments

formula

(formula)
Environmental predictors for this process' environmental-response function, evaluated against the env data. Default NULL uses ~. (all available environmental covariates).

func

(function)
Mechanistic process equation, e.g. growth, mortality, regeneration, or competition, or a custom function with the same arguments. Required.

initSpecies

(matrix)
Optional custom initial values for the species-specific process parameters. Default NULL draws random initial values.

initEnv

(list)
Optional custom initial values for the parameters of the environmental-response network/regression. Default NULL draws random initial values. For the linear/logistic response (no hidden) this is a matrix with one row per species and one column per term of formula (the intercept first when the formula has one). Without it the mortality response starts at about 2 % per time step (intercept qlogis(0.02), other weights 0; with hidden layers the output bias carries it) and the other processes at torch's random start; e.g. initEnv = matrix(c(-3, 0), N_species, 2, byrow = TRUE) for ~ 1 + temp starts mortality at 5 %.

hidden

(integer())
Hidden-layer sizes of the feed-forward neural network that replaces the environmental-response function (Level 1 hybrid). Default NULL keeps the environmental response mechanistic (linear/logistic).

optimizeSpecies

(logical(1))
Should the species-specific process parameters be estimated during fit()? Default FALSE.

optimizeEnv

(logical(1))
Should the parameters of the environmental-response function be estimated during fit()? Default TRUE.

inputNN, outputNN

Not used in 0.2.0: the input dimension of the environmental-response network always follows from formula and env, and its output dimension is the number of species. Leave at NULL.

dispersion_parameter

(numeric(1))
Initial dispersion parameter of the negative binomial distribution used to sample recruits (the size theta), or its fixed value with optimizeTheta = FALSE. Only used when this process is the regeneration process. See recruitment.

NN

(nn_module)
Optional custom torch module overriding the default environmental-response network architecture.

upper, lower

(numeric())
Boundaries (natural scale) for the species-specific process parameters, one value per parameter of the process. They are guard rails that keep the optimiser inside the range in which the equations stay meaningful, not ranges taken from the data, and fit() does not move them. The defaults, as lower / upper: growth c(0.01, 0.01) / c(0.99, 4.0) (light requirement of the shade response, size decay); mortality c(-10, -10, -10) / c(10, 10, 10) (the shade, size and growth coefficients of the logit); regeneration 0.01 / 0.99 (light requirement); competition c(0.3, 0.0) / c(log(2.3), 2.0) (height parameter, competition strength), where the height parameter is capped so that no species grows taller than 130 m (see height()). A parameter that ends a fit at its bound is not identified by the data; widening the bounds is a decision for 0.2.1.

dropout

(numeric(1))
Dropout rate of the environmental-response network. Ignored unless hidden is set.

sample_regeneration

(logical(1))
Should recruits actually be sampled from the negative binomial regeneration distribution (TRUE), or only its expectation used (FALSE)? Only used when this process is the regeneration process. With FALSE the expected number of recruits per patch is rounded, so wherever it is below 0.5 no recruit enters at all: a silent zero for sparse species on small patches. See recruitment.

n_quantiles

(integer(1))
Number of height classes used to discretize cohorts when computing shading/light availability. Only used when this process is the competition process and continuous = FALSE.

continuous

(logical(1))
Compute shading continuously for every pair of cohorts (TRUE) instead of binning cohorts into n_quantiles height classes (FALSE, default). Only used when this process is the competition process.

light_mask

(logical(1))
Take the height quantiles of the binned competition over the LIVE cohorts only. The cohort dimension is padded to the widest site x patch in the batch and an empty slot has height 0.001, so with enough padding every live cohort is searchsorted into the top bin, where nothing shades anything: measured on a 251 m2/ha stand of ten live cohorts, 100 padded slots put all ten at light 1.00. Only the quantile INPUT is masked, so every cohort keeps its real height as the bin query. TRUE is the default since 0.2.0, because the padded width is set by the widest site in the BATCH: the same stand of ten cohorts gets light 1.00 throughout beside a neighbour holding a hundred, and its correct gradient down to 0.159 beside a neighbour holding ten. Batch composition is not part of the model, so the unmasked quantile made the fitted objective depend on batchsize. FALSE reproduces results published before 0.2.0. Ignored when continuous = TRUE, which compares pairs and is correct at any padding.

custom_parameters

(named list or NULL)
Extra parameters that a custom func needs, declared here so they are registered on the model by finn(), optimised jointly by fit() (when trainable), and round-tripped by torch_save()/torch_load(). Each element is either a numeric vector (a trainable parameter with that starting value) or a list with init (numeric, length 1 or N_species) and optional trainable (logical, default TRUE; FALSE makes it a fixed buffer). The custom function accesses each as self[[name]]. Parameterise in the unconstrained space and apply any link inside the function (e.g. store log K and use exp(self$logK)), mirroring FINN's own par_*_unconstrained convention.

mortality_draw

(character(1))
How the number of dead trees is drawn from the cohort's mortality probability. Only used when this process is the mortality process. "binomial" (default since 0.2.0) is torch's exact binomial sampler: integer-valued, exact in both moments, at constant memory. It has no gradient of its own, which costs nothing under fit(rb_gradient = TRUE) (the default), where the gradient is taken through the expected number of deaths. Under fit(rb_gradient = FALSE) there is no such path, and "binomial" falls back to the "gamma" draw. "bernoulli" gives each tree of the cohort its own reparameterised Bernoulli trial (binomial_from_bernoulli()), which is integer-valued, matches the binomial in both moments – measured 12.011 / 8.387 against an exact 12.000 / 8.400 at n = 40, p = 0.3 – and keeps a gradient path to p through a straight-through sigmoid. It expands each cell to the largest cohort in the batch, so its memory grows with the largest trees value in the data. "poisson" draws a Bernoulli where the cohort holds one tree or fewer and a Poisson capped at the cohort size otherwise: integer-valued, exact in expectation for small n*p, and no pathwise gradient – which costs nothing now that fit(rb_gradient = TRUE) takes the gradient through the expectation anyway. The Bernoulli branch matters because capping a Poisson at a one-tree cohort delivers only 88 % of the calibrated probability at the p = 0.26 of a suppressed stem. "gamma" (the behaviour of every published FINN result) matches a Gamma to the binomial's first two moments and rsample()s it, which gives a pathwise gradient – the hazard a discrete draw does not cover – but the forward pass rounds that draw straight-through, so the gradient flows through a quantity the simulation discards and the rounded count delivers a measured 0.68-0.72 of the calibrated deaths for one-tree cohorts at annual probabilities of 0.01-0.10. See binomial_from_poisson() for the measured effect on the simulated stand.

regeneration_sampler

(character(1))
How recruits are drawn from the negative binomial. Only used when this process is the regeneration process and sample_regeneration = TRUE. "refined" (default since 0.2.0) samples exactly below lambda = 2 and drops both guards below, neither of which applies to torch_poisson; see rnbinom_torch_refined(). Above lambda = 2 it is still the floored Gaussian draw, which delivers about half a recruit per draw too few (measured over 1e6 draws: -0.43 at lambda = 2.5, -0.50 from lambda = 20, against about 0 with rounding). Rounding instead of flooring is planned for 0.2.1; it changes results, so it is not in this release. "gaussian" (the behaviour of every published FINN result) offsets the Gamma draw by +0.001, clamps the probability at 1e-4 and pushes the result through lambda + eps*sqrt(lambda). The offset and the clamp guard the Gaussian branch against a negative draw and against a NaN gradient through log(0); together they are a recruitment FLOOR of 0.0011 per cell-year, which at a FINN patch of 0.0168 ha is 0.066 recruits ha^-1 yr^-1 per species – over a pool of a hundred-odd species, as large as a temperate inventory's whole ingrowth.

growth_scale

(numeric(1) or NULL)
Overrides the growth_scale default of the process func. Only used when this process is the mortality process and func declares that argument. NULL (the default) keeps the function's own default, which for mortality() is 0.01 – growth enters the logit in %/yr. growth_scale = 1 feeds it the raw annual relative rate, the behaviour of 0.1.0. The value is set as the function's formal rather than passed down the forward pass, so a custom mortality func without the argument keeps working unchanged.

cap, prior, prior_lambda

The Beverton-Holt cap of regeneration_capped(): cap = "all" (default, one cap shared by all species) or "species"; prior = "max_obs_recruits" (default, the largest observed recruitment rate in the fitted data, recruits per ha and year) or a positive number; prior_lambda (default 0.1) the strength of the pull of log K towards log prior. See regeneration_capped(). Only used when this process is the regeneration process and its func uses the cap.

theta_floor

(numeric(1))
Lower bound on the negative-binomial recruit dispersion par_theta_recruits, applied wherever it is read: the recruit draw and the regeneration likelihood. Default 0.5 since 0.2.0; 0 or NULL leaves it unbounded, as in 0.1.0. Only used when this object is the regeneration process.

theta is trained, and it collapses, because lowering it widens the regeneration likelihood and so cheapens that term without improving the predicted mean. The same parameter sets the variance of the simulated recruit draw, mu + mu^2/theta, which then turns bursty: on the German NFI it reached 0.035 by epoch 50 and the simulated stand overshot observed recruitment 133-fold, with basal-area and stem losses flat until epoch 25 and running away after. The Beverton-Holt cap does not prevent this – it bounds the mean, and the variance around a capped mean is still K + K^2/theta.

The floor keeps the fit stable, and in one converged pair of fits on the German national forest inventory it calibrated the recruitment level as well as a fixed theta: out of sample on a spatially blocked holdout, 1.06 times the observed level after 2000 epochs (about 126 000 optimizer steps) against 1.04 for optimizeTheta = FALSE. A fit stopped early is different: after 50 of those epochs (3 150 optimizer steps) the floored theta still put the level about 12 times too high, a fixed theta 2 to 3 times. Read the level only once the parameters have settled, or fix theta for short fits. See recruitment.

optimizeTheta

(logical(1))
Should the recruit dispersion par_theta_recruits be estimated during fit()? Default TRUE. With FALSE it stays at dispersion_parameter for the whole fit (a buffer, not a parameter), in the recruit draw and in the regeneration likelihood alike; theta_floor still applies. Only used when this process is the regeneration process.

Use FALSE for short fits, or when the recruitment level should not depend on how long the fit runs: a trained theta falls on sparse recruitment data, and with the floor (theta_floor) the level is right only once the fit has converged, while a fixed theta gets there sooner. dispersion_parameter = 1 is FINN's start value; on the German national forest inventory it matched the floored theta at convergence. A higher value such as 50 brings the recruit draw close to a Poisson draw: the variance mu + mu^2/theta approaches mu while the expected count per patch mu stays small against theta (at theta = 50 the excess is 2 % of the mean at mu = 1 and 20 % at mu = 10). Per-patch recruit counts are usually small enough for that; larger counts need a larger value. See recruitment.

mortality_floor, mortality_ceiling

(numeric(1))
The interval the per-cohort mortality probability is clamped to per simulation step, before the death draw. Only used when this process is the mortality process; the per-tree mortality loss is not bounded by either.

The defaults are 0.001 and 0.999 (0.1 % and 99.9 % per step). Until 0.2.0 the interval was hard-coded to [0.01, 0.99], which is why a simulated low-mortality stand – a mature unthinned stand, a slow-growing species, an equilibrium run – lost stems the observations did not: at a 1 % floor it loses 1 % of every cohort per step however low the fitted rate.

The floor exists because binomial_from_gamma()'s shape n*p/(1-p) degenerates as p -> 0. Measured with that draw, it stays finite with an unbiased mean gradient down to 1e-4, but single-draw gradients grow heavy-tailed as n*p shrinks – the largest per-tree gradient is about ten times the old default's at 1e-3 and about a hundred times at 1e-4 – so 1e-3 is the lowest tested value and is the new default.

reg_floor

(numeric)
A small recruitment that every species gets in every patch and time step, whatever the light and the environment, in trees per ha and time step. Only used when this process is the regeneration process (regeneration(), regeneration_capped(), regeneration_adult() and regeneration_adult_effect() add it to their expected recruitment: mean = regP * exp(env) + reg_floor). Default 1e-3, which keeps the recruitment likelihood finite where the light response closes and adds next to nothing. One value for all species or one per species. Before 0.2.0 the floor was hard-coded to 0.2, which with many species adds a large recruitment that does not depend on anything (65 species x 0.2 = 13 trees per ha and year); models saved before then keep that value when reloaded. finn(reg_floor = ), the argument of earlier versions, is still accepted with a warning and overrides this value.

Value

A list of class "process" containing the process definition and associated parameters, to be passed as mortality_process, growth_process, regeneration_process, or competition_process to finn().

Details

Each demographic process in FINN is the product of (i) a process equation func that operates on the cohort state (dbh, number of trees, available light, species) and species-specific process parameters, and (ii) a species- and process-specific environmental-response function that maps site-level environmental predictors to a scalar effect on the process (see finn() for the underlying equations). createProcess() configures both parts:

  • func implements the mechanistic process equation itself. The package's default process functions (growth, mortality, regeneration, competition) reproduce the equations described by Pichler & Käber (2026); a custom function with the same arguments can be passed instead to use a different functional form while keeping the process embedded in, and jointly calibrated with, the rest of the model.

  • The environmental-response function is, by default (hidden = NULL), a linear/logistic niche function with one coefficient per environmental covariate (named in formula) and per species, comparable to a classic species distribution model. Setting hidden to a vector of hidden-layer sizes (e.g. c(25L)) instead replaces this function with a feed-forward neural network, while func and the species-specific process parameters remain mechanistic – the "Level 1" hybridization described in the paper.

formula selects which columns of the env data (passed to fit() or predict.finn_class()) enter the environmental-response function; initSpecies/initEnv allow supplying custom starting values for the process parameters/environmental-response model instead of the package's random initialization; optimizeSpecies/optimizeEnv control whether these parameters are estimated during fit() or held fixed at their initial values; and upper/lower set box constraints (on the natural process-parameter scale) within which the species-specific process parameters are constrained during optimization.

References

Pichler, M., & Käber, Y. (2026). Inferring processes within dynamic forest models using hybrid modelling. Methods in Ecology and Evolution. doi:10.1111/2041-210x.70347

See also

createHybrid(), finn(), recruitment for the recruitment options and how to combine them

Examples

# A process is a recipe: createProcess() needs neither data nor torch, and the
# predictors named in `formula` are looked up in `env` when the model is
# fitted or simulated. Here: growth responding to temperature and precipitation
growth_process <- createProcess(formula = ~ temp + prec, func = growth)
class(growth_process)
#> [1] "process"
deparse(growth_process$formula)
#> [1] "~temp + prec"

# the same equation with its species parameters estimated as well (by default
# only the environmental response is), and a quadratic temperature response
growth_process <- createProcess(~ temp + I(temp^2) + prec, func = growth,
                                optimizeSpecies = TRUE)

# level-1 hybrid: the environmental response of mortality as a small neural
# network with two hidden layers; the mortality equation stays mechanistic
mortality_process <- createProcess(~ temp + prec, func = mortality,
                                   hidden = c(16L, 16L), dropout = 0.1)
#> Neural Network detected...

# the regeneration process with a smaller recruitment floor, a cap per
# species and a fixed recruit dispersion
regeneration_process <- createProcess(~ temp, func = regeneration_capped,
                                      reg_floor = 1e-4, cap = "species",
                                      optimizeTheta = FALSE)

# competition takes no environment; continuous = TRUE compares every pair of
# cohorts instead of binning them into height classes
competition_process <- createProcess(func = competition, continuous = TRUE)

# the processes become a model in finn(), here for the 11 species of the
# bundled Oregon FIA data (?fia_obs_dt), whose env table has `temp` and `prec`
m <- finn(N_species = 11, recruits_dbh = 12.9,
          growth_process       = growth_process,
          mortality_process    = mortality_process,
          regeneration_process = regeneration_process,
          competition_process  = competition_process)
# the species parameters of growth: light requirement and size decay
head(as.matrix(m$par_growth), 3)
#>           [,1]       [,2]
#> [1,] 0.4952571 0.05029631
#> [2,] 0.4675127 0.04575275
#> [3,] 0.5246698 0.04777756
